title: Propylthiouracil: Thyroid Control With Liver Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Propylthiouracil reduces thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion but carries a serious risk of severe liver injury. It is generally reserved for selected situations, including when methimazole is unsuitable and in specific early-pregnancy contexts.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, anorexia, pruritus, right-upper-quadrant pain, or severe fatigue can signal liver injury.
Fever or sore throat can signal agranulocytosis.
priorities: Verify indication and pregnancy context.
Escalate liver-injury symptoms or fever/sore throat immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend thyroid function, clinical hyperthyroid symptoms, CBC when clinically indicated, and liver-symptom surveillance.
interventions: Administer on schedule and reinforce that symptom improvement does not justify abrupt self-discontinuation.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling carries a boxed warning for severe liver injury and acute liver failure.
Pregnancy-specific drug selection requires prescriber management.
teaching: Report jaundice, dark urine, fever, or sore throat promptly.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; suspected liver injury or agranulocytosis requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Treating PTU as interchangeable with methimazole in every patient without considering liver risk and pregnancy context.
oneLinePearl: PTU controls thyroid hormone, but the liver warning controls the safety plan.

title: Hydrocortisone: Replacement, Stress, and Adrenal Safety
bottomLine: Hydrocortisone can be replacement therapy for adrenal insufficiency or higher-dose anti-inflammatory therapy. Abrupt interruption after chronic exposure can precipitate adrenal insufficiency; acute adrenal crisis requires rapid ordered steroid and supportive treatment.
recognize: Hypotension, weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, or shock may signal adrenal crisis.
Long-term corticosteroid exposure can cause hyperglycemia, infection risk, osteoporosis, mood changes, and HPA-axis suppression.
priorities: Confirm whether the patient uses chronic replacement/steroid therapy and whether stress-dose instructions apply.
Escalate suspected adrenal crisis immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, glucose, electrolytes, infection signs, mental status, and response to therapy.
interventions: Administer replacement or emergency hydrocortisone exactly as ordered; chronic therapy is tapered when clinically required rather than abruptly stopped.
medicationSafety: Current hydrocortisone labeling warns about HPA-axis suppression and secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
Steroids can mask infection and raise glucose.
redFlags: Severe vomiting with inability to take replacement
teaching: Do not stop chronic steroids suddenly; follow sick-day/stress instructions and carry emergency information if prescribed.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; suspected adrenal crisis requires emergency escalation.
examTrap: Holding a chronic adrenal-replacement steroid because the patient is acutely ill and not eating well.
oneLinePearl: Stress increases cortisol need—adrenal insufficiency is the wrong time to lose steroid coverage.
sourceBasis: DailyMed hydrocortisone sodium succinate labeling current 2026

title: Fludrocortisone: Mineralocorticoid Replacement and Volume Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fludrocortisone increases sodium retention and potassium loss. Monitor blood pressure, edema, weight, and potassium so mineralocorticoid replacement does not become volume overload or hypokalemia.
recognize: Hypertension, edema, rapid weight gain, weakness, or dysrhythmia can reflect excessive mineralocorticoid effect.
priorities: Trend BP, weight, edema, and electrolytes.
Escalate severe hypertension, pulmonary edema, or symptomatic hypokalemia.
assessMonitor: BP, sodium, potassium, edema, weight, heart-failure symptoms.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce prescribed sodium/potassium guidance.
medicationSafety: Current labeling identifies hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, and excessive weight gain as signs of excess exposure.
teaching: Track BP/weight if instructed and report swelling or muscle weakness.
delegationScope: Routine weights/BP may be delegated with thresholds; abnormal trends require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Encouraging unrestricted sodium intake in a patient developing edema and hypertension on fludrocortisone.
oneLinePearl: Fludrocortisone holds sodium and loses potassium—watch pressure, weight, and K.

title: Denosumab: Bone Protection With Calcium Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Denosumab suppresses osteoclast activity and reduces fracture risk, but hypocalcemia can be severe—especially in advanced CKD/CKD-mineral bone disorder. Calcium status and dental/infection concerns matter before and after treatment.
recognize: Perioral tingling, cramps, tetany, confusion, or seizure can signal hypocalcemia.
Jaw pain or nonhealing oral lesions raise concern for osteonecrosis of the jaw.
priorities: Verify calcium/vitamin-D plan and renal/CKD-MBD risk before treatment.
Escalate symptomatic hypocalcemia or jaw complications.
assessMonitor: Calcium, renal/CKD-MBD context, dental symptoms, infection/skin symptoms, fracture history.
interventions: Reinforce calcium/vitamin-D supplementation as prescribed and dental preventive care.
medicationSafety: The June 2026 U.S. Prolia label carries a boxed warning for severe hypocalcemia in advanced kidney disease.
Do not delay or stop ongoing osteoporosis therapy without prescriber planning because rebound fracture risk can occur after discontinuation.
teaching: Maintain prescribed calcium/vitamin D and report tingling, cramps, jaw pain, or dental problems.
delegationScope: Administration requires facility competency; symptomatic hypocalcemia requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Giving denosumab without addressing low calcium in a patient with advanced CKD.
oneLinePearl: Denosumab protects bone but can drop calcium dangerously in advanced kidney disease.

title: Calcitonin Salmon: Calcium Lowering and Long-Term Reassessment
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Calcitonin salmon can lower calcium and is used in selected bone/calcium disorders. Hypocalcemia, hypersensitivity, nasal effects for spray products, and periodic reassessment of prolonged therapy are key safety issues.
recognize: Tingling, cramps, or tetany can signal hypocalcemia.
Current labeling notes a possible association between malignancy and prolonged use, so ongoing need should be reassessed.
priorities: Review calcium and indication; verify injectable versus nasal formulation.
Escalate severe hypersensitivity or symptomatic hypocalcemia.
assessMonitor: Calcium, symptom response, nasal mucosa if spray used, and ongoing indication.
interventions: Use product-specific administration and rotate nostrils for nasal therapy as directed.
medicationSafety: Patients with fish/salmon hypersensitivity may be at increased allergy risk.
Long-term need should be periodically reevaluated.
teaching: Report severe allergy symptoms or muscle cramping/tingling.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; severe allergy or calcium symptoms require escalation.
examTrap: Assuming calcitonin is a harmless chronic supplement requiring no ongoing reassessment.
oneLinePearl: Calcitonin lowers calcium—monitor calcium and keep asking whether therapy is still needed.

title: Lamotrigine: Rash Is a Safety Signal
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Lamotrigine is used for epilepsy and bipolar maintenance, but new rash can represent life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Slow titration and immediate evaluation of rash are central safety principles.
recognize: Serious rash risk is higher early in treatment and with excessive starting dose/rapid escalation.
Mucosal lesions, blistering, facial swelling, fever, or systemic illness make a rash especially concerning.
priorities: Verify titration history and interacting medications such as valproate.
Escalate any new rash promptly and urgently for mucosal involvement or systemic symptoms.
assessMonitor: Skin/mucosa, fever, mood/suicidality, seizure control, adherence/titration.
interventions: Do not independently restart at the prior full dose after a significant interruption; follow prescriber/product re-titration guidance.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling carries a boxed warning for serious skin rashes including SJS/TEN.
Valproate can increase lamotrigine exposure and rash risk.
teaching: Report any new rash immediately, especially early in therapy.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; rash assessment and treatment decisions require licensed/provider escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient that an early lamotrigine rash is expected and can wait until the next appointment.
oneLinePearl: With lamotrigine, rash is never a casual finding.

title: Topiramate: Think Acidosis, Stones, and Cognition
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Topiramate can treat seizures and prevent migraine but may cause metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, cognitive slowing, weight loss, and acute ocular complications. Hydration and bicarbonate/renal awareness matter.
recognize: Fatigue, hyperventilation, anorexia, or arrhythmia can accompany metabolic acidosis.
Sudden eye pain or blurred vision can indicate acute angle-closure glaucoma.
priorities: Review bicarbonate/renal history and hydration status.
Escalate acute eye symptoms, severe acidosis symptoms, or major neurologic change.
assessMonitor: Bicarbonate, renal function, weight, cognition, vision symptoms, seizure/migraine response.
interventions: Encourage hydration when appropriate and not fluid restricted; taper rather than abruptly stop when discontinuing anticonvulsant therapy.
medicationSafety: Current labeling warns about metabolic acidosis and increased kidney-stone risk, especially with other acidosis-promoting conditions or ketogenic diet.
teaching: Report sudden vision changes and maintain prescribed hydration.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; acute ocular or acid-base symptoms require escalation.
examTrap: Ignoring persistent low bicarbonate because the patient's migraines improved.
oneLinePearl: Topiramate can change thinking, bicarbonate, and stone risk.

title: Sumatriptan: Migraine Rescue With Vascular Contraindications
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sumatriptan treats acute migraine through 5-HT1 agonism but can cause vasoconstriction. Coronary/cerebrovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, interacting triptan/ergot exposure, and atypical neurologic symptoms require careful review.
recognize: Chest pressure after a triptan may be benign but ischemic symptoms must not be dismissed.
A first or atypical 'migraine' with focal neurologic deficit requires stroke evaluation rather than automatic triptan treatment.
priorities: Confirm migraine diagnosis/history and vascular contraindications.
Escalate ischemic chest pain, focal neurologic deficit, or severe hypertension.
assessMonitor: Headache response, BP, chest symptoms, neurologic status, frequency of rescue use.
interventions: Administer within the prescribed acute-migraine plan and respect spacing from other triptans/ergot drugs.
medicationSafety: Current labeling contraindicates use in ischemic CAD/coronary vasospasm and with recent other triptan or ergot exposure.
Serotonin syndrome is possible with serotonergic co-medications.
teaching: Use only for the prescribed migraine pattern and seek urgent care for chest pain or new neurologic deficits.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; atypical headache or vascular symptoms require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Giving sumatriptan to a patient with new unilateral weakness because they have a history of migraines.
oneLinePearl: Triptans treat migraine, not unexplained focal neurologic deficits.

title: Baclofen: Sedation and Dangerous Abrupt Withdrawal
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Baclofen reduces spasticity through GABA-B activity. Sedation and weakness matter during treatment, while abrupt withdrawal can cause hallucinations, seizures, severe hyperthermia/rigidity, and life-threatening deterioration.
recognize: Drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, confusion, and falls can occur during therapy.
Abrupt cessation can produce hallucinations and seizures; severe withdrawal can become systemic.
priorities: Assess sedation, falls, renal context, and adherence.
Do not abruptly discontinue chronic therapy; escalate suspected withdrawal.
assessMonitor: Mental status, spasticity, gait/fall risk, renal function, withdrawal symptoms.
interventions: Use gradual tapering when discontinuation is ordered.
medicationSafety: Current labeling warns against abrupt withdrawal because hallucinations and seizures have occurred.
teaching: Do not stop baclofen suddenly and report missed doses plus new confusion or hallucinations.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; withdrawal or CNS depression requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Stopping baclofen abruptly because the patient appears excessively sleepy without first escalating for a safe plan.
oneLinePearl: Baclofen can sedate on therapy and destabilize dangerously off therapy.

title: Pyridostigmine: Improve Strength Without Cholinergic Crisis
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pyridostigmine improves neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia gravis. Too little medication can worsen myasthenic weakness, while excessive cholinergic activity can also cause profound weakness—plus secretions, diarrhea, cramping, bradycardia, and respiratory compromise.
recognize: Cholinergic excess may include salivation, sweating, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, miosis, bradycardia, and increasing weakness.
Either myasthenic or cholinergic crisis can threaten breathing; bedside guessing should not delay escalation.
priorities: Assess respiratory effort, swallowing, secretions, heart rate, and recent dosing.
Escalate rapidly worsening weakness or respiratory compromise regardless of suspected cause.
assessMonitor: Respiratory function, bulbar symptoms, strength, secretions, bowel symptoms, HR, medication timing.
interventions: Time doses consistently and around meals/activity when prescribed to optimize swallowing/function.
medicationSafety: Overdosage can cause cholinergic crisis with increasing muscle weakness and respiratory involvement.
Anticholinergic rescue decisions require provider/emergency protocol, not routine self-adjustment.
teaching: Take doses on schedule and seek urgent care for worsening swallowing or breathing rather than doubling medication.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; crisis differentiation and respiratory deterioration require immediate RN/provider/emergency escalation.
examTrap: Giving an extra pyridostigmine dose automatically to every myasthenia patient who becomes weaker.
oneLinePearl: In myasthenia, both under-treatment and cholinergic excess can look weak—breathing comes first.
